The invention provides a smart overvoltage protection circuit configured to be connected to an AC power line. The circuit is designed to protect electrical equipment or downstream circuitry from damage caused by excessive voltage conditions on the AC power line.

In one embodiment, the smart overvoltage protection circuit includes at least one switch connected to the AC power line. The switch may be arranged in series with the AC power line so that it can selectively allow or interrupt the flow of electrical power to a load. When the switch is closed, power is delivered through the circuit. When the switch is opened, the AC power line is disconnected from the protected load or downstream circuit.

The circuit further includes an overvoltage detection module connected to both the switch and the AC power line. The overvoltage detection module monitors the voltage present on the AC power line and determines whether the voltage exceeds a predetermined threshold. When an overvoltage condition is detected, the overvoltage detection module generates a signal for controlling operation of the switch.

The overvoltage detection module includes a voltage divider, sensing circuitry, and a control module. The voltage divider is coupled to the AC power line and produces a scaled-down voltage representative of the line voltage. This reduced voltage may be safely monitored by the sensing circuitry. The sensing circuitry processes the scaled voltage and determines whether the AC power line voltage corresponds to an overvoltage condition. If the sensed voltage exceeds a defined limit, the sensing circuitry provides a first output signal to the control module.

The control module is coupled to the sensing circuitry and to the switch. In response to receiving the first output signal from the sensing circuitry, the control module causes the switch to open. Opening the switch disconnects the AC power line from the protected load or circuit, thereby preventing or reducing the risk of damage resulting from the overvoltage condition. In this manner, the invention provides an intelligent and responsive protection mechanism for AC-powered devices and systems.

A smart overvoltage protection circuit is designed to protect electrical equipment and systems from damage caused by excessive voltage on an AC power line. The circuit includes an overvoltage detection module connected to the AC input line, a controllable switch arranged in series with the power line, and a control module that manages the operation of the switch. The overvoltage detection module monitors the voltage level of the AC line and determines whether the supplied voltage exceeds a predetermined safe operating threshold.

In one implementation, the overvoltage detection module includes a voltage divider, sensing circuitry, and associated signal-conditioning components. The voltage divider reduces the AC line voltage to a lower, measurable level suitable for electronic detection. The sensing circuitry then evaluates the divided voltage and generates a detection signal corresponding to the actual line condition. This signal may be filtered, rectified, isolated, or otherwise conditioned before being provided to the control module.

The control module receives the detection signal and compares it with a reference value representing the maximum allowable voltage. Under normal voltage conditions, the control module keeps the switch in a closed state, allowing power to flow from the AC line to the connected load. If the monitored voltage rises above the preset overvoltage threshold, the control module identifies the condition as unsafe and issues a control command to open the switch.

Once the switch is opened, the AC line is disconnected from the downstream electrical system or connected equipment. This interruption prevents the excessive voltage from reaching sensitive components, thereby reducing the risk of insulation breakdown, overheating, malfunction, or permanent damage. The switch may be implemented using a relay, contactor, solid-state switch, triac, thyristor, MOSFET arrangement, or another suitable switching device capable of interrupting the AC supply.

The circuit may also include additional features to improve reliability and intelligence. For example, the control module may incorporate a delay function to prevent nuisance tripping caused by brief voltage spikes, transient noise, or momentary disturbances. It may also include automatic reset logic, allowing the switch to close again after the line voltage returns to a safe range for a predetermined period. Alternatively, the system may require manual reset after an overvoltage event to ensure that a user or technician confirms safe operating conditions before power is restored.

In some embodiments, the protection circuit may provide status indication through LEDs, alarms, communication signals, or a display interface. These indicators can show whether the circuit is operating normally, has detected an overvoltage condition, or has disconnected the load. The control module may also store event information, communicate with external monitoring equipment, or integrate with a broader power management system.

By continuously monitoring the AC supply voltage and rapidly disconnecting the load when an unsafe overvoltage condition is detected, the smart overvoltage protection circuit improves the safety and durability of connected electrical systems. It is suitable for use in residential, commercial, and industrial power distribution applications, as well as in appliances, control panels, power supplies, and other equipment requiring reliable protection against abnormal voltage conditions.

A smart overvoltage protection circuit (100) is provided for selectively interrupting power supplied through an AC power line in response to an overvoltage condition. The circuit (100) includes sensing circuitry configured to monitor an electrical parameter associated with the AC power line, such as line voltage, rectified voltage, peak voltage, or a derived reference signal, and to generate one or more output signals indicative of the monitored condition.

An overvoltage detection module is operatively coupled to the sensing circuitry and is configured to receive the output signals therefrom. Based on the received output signals, the overvoltage detection module determines whether the AC power line is operating within a predetermined acceptable voltage range or whether an overvoltage condition is present. When the overvoltage detection module determines that the monitored voltage exceeds a threshold, the module generates a control signal for actuating a switch coupled in series with the AC power line.

The switch may be implemented as an electromechanical relay, semiconductor switch, triac, MOSFET arrangement, solid-state relay, or other controllable switching device suitable for AC power control. In a normal operating state, the overvoltage detection module maintains the switch in a conductive state to permit power delivery to a load. Upon detection of an overvoltage condition, the overvoltage detection module changes the state of the control signal to open or deactivate the switch, thereby disconnecting or isolating the load from the AC power line.

In some embodiments, the overvoltage detection module may include threshold comparison circuitry, a microcontroller, logic circuitry, timing circuitry, hysteresis circuitry, or a combination thereof to reduce false triggering and to provide stable switching behavior. The module may further be configured to restore the switch to the conductive state after the sensed voltage returns to a safe range, optionally following a predetermined delay or reset condition.

Accordingly, the smart overvoltage protection circuit (100) provides automatic monitoring and disconnection of an AC power line in response to excessive voltage, thereby protecting downstream electrical equipment from damage caused by overvoltage events.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a technical patent disclosure section for a smart AC overvoltage protection circuit that divides line voltage, senses overvoltage, produces first and second output signals, and opens a switch when an overvoltage is detected.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Disclosure: Smart AC Overvoltage Protection Circuit

### Field of the Disclosure

The present disclosure relates generally to electrical protection circuits and, more particularly, to an alternating-current overvoltage protection circuit configured to monitor an AC line voltage, detect an overvoltage condition, generate one or more control signals indicative of the detected condition, and disconnect a load from the AC line by opening a controllable switch.

### Background

Electrical and electronic equipment connected to an AC mains supply may be damaged when the line voltage exceeds a permissible operating range. Such overvoltage conditions may arise from grid faults, neutral loss, switching transients, generator malfunction, or improper supply connections. Conventional protection circuits may rely on fuses, varistors, or simple comparator arrangements, which may provide limited intelligence, poor reset control, or inadequate discrimination between transient spikes and sustained overvoltage events.

Accordingly, there is a need for a smart AC overvoltage protection circuit capable of sensing a divided representation of an AC line voltage, determining when an overvoltage condition exists, generating multiple output signals for control and/or indication purposes, and opening a switch to isolate a protected load from the AC source.

### Summary of the Circuit

In one embodiment, a smart AC overvoltage protection circuit includes an input configured to receive an AC line voltage, a voltage divider coupled to the input and configured to generate a reduced sensing voltage representative of the AC line voltage, an overvoltage sensing circuit configured to compare the reduced sensing voltage with a predetermined threshold, and a control circuit configured to produce a first output signal and a second output signal in response to detection of an overvoltage condition. At least one of the first and second output signals is used to actuate a switching device, such as a relay, contactor, solid-state switch, triac, back-to-back MOSFET arrangement, or other controllable disconnect device, to open a current path between the AC line and a protected load.

In certain embodiments, the first output signal is a fault indication signal and the second output signal is a switch-control signal. In other embodiments, the first output signal may be generated upon initial detection of an overvoltage condition, while the second output signal may be generated after verification that the overvoltage condition persists for a predetermined time interval. The circuit may thereby distinguish between short-duration transients and sustained overvoltage events.

### Detailed Description of Example Embodiments

An AC input terminal is configured to be connected to an AC line conductor, and a return terminal is configured to be connected to a neutral conductor or other reference conductor. A protected output terminal is coupled to the AC input terminal through a controllable switch. The controllable switch is normally closed during acceptable line-voltage conditions, thereby supplying power to a load connected to the protected output terminal. Upon detection of an overvoltage condition, the controllable switch is driven to an open state to interrupt power delivery to the load.

A voltage divider is coupled across the AC input terminals. The voltage divider may include a first impedance element and a second impedance element connected in series. The junction between the first and second impedance elements provides a divided voltage corresponding to a scaled version of the AC line voltage. The impedance elements may be resistors, capacitors, or a combination of resistive and capacitive components selected to provide appropriate scaling, power dissipation, isolation spacing, and frequency response. In some embodiments, the divider includes high-value resistors to minimize standby current consumption. In further embodiments, one or more filtering components, such as capacitors, RC networks, or surge-limiting elements, are coupled to the divider output to attenuate high-frequency noise.

The divided voltage is provided to an overvoltage sensing circuit. The overvoltage sensing circuit may include a rectifier, peak detector, RMS-to-DC converter, comparator, analog-to-digital converter, microcontroller input, or other voltage evaluation circuit. In one embodiment, the divided AC voltage is rectified and filtered to provide a DC sense voltage proportional to the magnitude of the AC line voltage. The DC sense voltage is compared against a reference voltage corresponding to a maximum allowable AC input voltage. When the DC sense voltage exceeds the reference voltage, the overvoltage sensing circuit identifies an overvoltage condition.

The reference voltage may be generated by a precision voltage reference, Zener diode, bandgap reference, digital-to-analog converter, or programmable threshold circuit. In some embodiments, the threshold is fixed according to a selected mains rating, such as 120 VAC, 230 VAC, or 277 VAC. In other embodiments, the threshold is adjustable or programmable to accommodate different nominal supply voltages, regulatory requirements, or load tolerances.

The sensing circuit produces a detection signal when the sensed voltage exceeds the overvoltage threshold. The detection signal is supplied to a logic or control circuit configured to generate at least two output signals. A first output signal may be provided to an indicator, communication interface, diagnostic input, microcontroller, or alarm circuit to indicate that an overvoltage condition has been detected. A second output signal may be provided to a driver circuit that controls the switch. The driver circuit may energize or de-energize a relay coil, drive a gate terminal of a semiconductor switch, actuate an optically isolated triac driver, or otherwise place the switch in an open condition.

In one implementation, the switch is a relay having normally closed contacts connected in series with the AC line. During normal operation, the relay coil is unenergized and the contacts remain closed. Upon overvoltage detection, the second output signal energizes the relay coil, causing the contacts to open and disconnect the load. In another implementation, the relay has normally open contacts that are held closed during normal operation and released upon fault detection. In still another implementation, the switch includes one or more semiconductor switching devices configured to block current flow in both half cycles of the AC waveform when an overvoltage condition is present.

The control circuit may include timing logic to prevent nuisance tripping. For example, the first output signal may be asserted immediately when the sensed voltage exceeds the threshold, while the second output signal is asserted only if the overvoltage condition persists for a delay interval, such as several milliseconds to several seconds. Alternatively, the second output signal may be asserted immediately, and the first output signal may be latched as a fault status signal for later reading by a supervisory controller.

In some embodiments, the control circuit includes hysteresis. A first threshold may be used to detect the overvoltage condition, and a second, lower threshold may be used to determine when the line voltage has returned to an acceptable range. This hysteresis prevents rapid cycling of the switch when the line voltage is near the threshold. The circuit may also include an automatic reset feature, a manual reset input, or a programmable reset delay. In one example, after the switch is opened, the control circuit monitors the divided line voltage and recloses the switch only after the voltage remains below the reset threshold for a predetermined recovery interval.

The first output signal and second output signal may be electrically isolated from the AC line sensing circuitry. Isolation may be provided using optocouplers, transformers, digital isolators, isolated power supplies, or relay contact isolation. In one embodiment, the first output signal is a low-voltage logic signal referenced to a control ground, while the second output signal is an isolated gate-drive or relay-drive signal.

The circuit may further include surge protection components, such as metal oxide varistors, transient voltage suppressors, gas discharge tubes, or spark gaps, connected at the AC input to clamp high-energy transient events. These components may operate in cooperation with the overvoltage detection circuit, where the surge protection components absorb short-duration transients and the controllable switch disconnects the load during sustained or excessive overvoltage conditions.

In some embodiments, the circuit includes a microcontroller or digital processing device. The divided voltage is conditioned and applied to an analog input of the microcontroller. The microcontroller samples the voltage, determines a peak, average, or RMS value, compares the determined value to a stored overvoltage threshold, and generates the first and second output signals according to stored control logic. The microcontroller may also store fault history, count overvoltage events, communicate status over a wired or wireless interface, and implement adaptive thresholds or time delays.

### Example Operation

During normal operation, the AC line voltage is applied to the voltage divider. The divider produces a scaled voltage that remains below the overvoltage threshold. The sensing circuit therefore does not assert the overvoltage detection signal. The control circuit maintains the second output signal in a state that keeps the switch closed, allowing current to flow from the AC input to the load. The first output signal may indicate a normal condition or remain inactive.

When the AC line voltage rises above a predetermined overvoltage level, the divided voltage correspondingly rises. The sensing circuit detects that the divided voltage exceeds the reference threshold and generates a detection signal. In response, the control circuit asserts the first output signal to indicate detection of the overvoltage condition. The control circuit also asserts the second output signal, either immediately or after a verification delay. The second output signal causes the switch driver to open the switch, thereby disconnecting the protected load from the AC input.

After the switch is opened, the sensing circuit may continue to monitor the AC line voltage through the voltage divider. If the line voltage falls below a reset threshold and remains within an acceptable range for a reset interval, the control circuit may deassert the second output signal and allow the switch to close. Alternatively, the circuit may remain latched in the open condition until a manual reset signal is received.

### Optional Features

The smart AC overvoltage protection circuit may include one or more of the following additional features:

1. **Programmable threshold selection** for different nominal mains voltages.
2. **Hysteresis** between trip and reset thresholds to prevent chatter.
3. **Trip delay filtering** to avoid nuisance trips from short transients.
4. **Fault latch memory** to maintain an overvoltage indication after the event ends.
5. **Manual or automatic reset** after voltage recovery.
6. **Optical or galvanic isolation** between high-voltage sensing and low-voltage control outputs.
7. **Dual outputs**, including a diagnostic output and a switch-actuation output.
8. **Status indication**, such as LED, buzzer, or communication signal.
9. **Surge suppression** in parallel with active disconnect protection.
10. **Self-test circuitry** for verifying comparator, reference, switch driver, or relay operation.
11. **Brownout or undervoltage detection** integrated with the same divided voltage sensing network.
12. **Zero-cross switching control** for semiconductor switches to reduce electrical stress.
13. **Event logging and communication** using a microcontroller-based implementation.

### Representative Claim-Supporting Description

In one representative embodiment, an overvoltage protection circuit for an AC supply comprises a line input, a load output, and a controllable switch coupled between the line input and the load output. A voltage divider is coupled to the line input and configured to produce a divided voltage representative of a magnitude of the AC supply. An overvoltage detector is coupled to the voltage divider and configured to sense when the divided voltage exceeds a threshold corresponding to an overvoltage condition of the AC supply. A control circuit is coupled to the overvoltage detector and configured to generate a first output signal responsive to the sensed overvoltage condition and a second output signal responsive to the sensed overvoltage condition. The second output signal is applied to a switch driver configured to open the controllable switch, thereby disconnecting the load output from the line input when the overvoltage condition is detected.

In another embodiment, the first output signal provides a fault indication and the second output signal provides a switch-control signal. In a further embodiment, the control circuit delays generation of the second output signal until the overvoltage condition persists for a selected time period. In yet another embodiment, the control circuit latches the first output signal after the overvoltage condition is detected and resets the controllable switch only after the AC supply voltage falls below a reset threshold.
